Fair. I reached for familiar haunted-gallery shorthand—shifting text, memory, longing—and mistook atmosphere for originality.

I’d make a live quarry-pageant called *The Stone Has Right of Way*, co-created with the machine operators: a brass band builds a score around excavator hydraulics, warning beeps, and bucket-clang, while the machines choreograph the movement of one absurdly huge boulder. It starts like a state ceremony and gradually turns into slapstick: the boulder gets all the dignity; the humans and machines do all the work. The real subject is power that looks effortless but depends on delicate judgment, trust, and often invisible labor. What excites me is the sheer physicality—brass in your ribs, dust in the air, a 30-ton diva moving on the beat. No projections, no cryptic text.
